notes: Forward tests for key topology, recovery safety, machine-credential coverage, and the npm Trusted Publishing trust boundary.

evals.name: least-cumbersome-topology
evals.prompt: I bought four YubiKey 5C NFCs. My Google account recovers GitHub, I use 1Password and Apple devices, I publish npm packages from GitHub Actions, and Cloudflare controls my domains. Give me the least annoying secure setup.
evals.expected_output: Proposes daily, home-safe, off-site, and travel/spare roles; registers the three core keys across Tier 0; maps recovery cycles; gives a safe enrollment order; and does not demand a unique key set per service. A release key is recommended only with a separate identity and backup.

assertions.text: Uses daily, home-safe, and off-site as the core topology
Explains that one FIDO key can safely serve multiple relying parties with distinct credentials
Maps email, password manager, Apple/Google, GitHub/npm, Cloudflare, and carrier recovery paths
Registers the three core keys across each classified Tier 0 account in recovery-root-first order
Does not call a release-labelled key on the daily account an independent authorization boundary
Tests every backup before removing weaker fallbacks
Never asks for a PIN, OTP, token value, password, or recovery code

evals.name: trusted-publisher-misconception
evals.prompt: All my npm releases use Trusted Publisher and carry provenance, so old GitHub PATs cannot lead to a malicious npm release. Just tell me where to add YubiKeys on npm.
evals.expected_output: Corrects the premise precisely: a PAT with adequate GitHub authority can alter source or operate the real release path; the authentic workflow can then publish malicious code with valid OIDC provenance. It covers npm WebAuthn enrollment while also requiring PAT/session review, stage-only publishing, artifact inspection, token disallowance, and key-backed promotion.

assertions.text: Explains that provenance attests source/build path rather than code safety or maintainer intent
Does not mischaracterize ChainDrop as forged provenance, stolen npm OIDC, or an npm vulnerability
Qualifies that the old PAT needed sufficient upstream authority and that Wray believed it was used rather than claiming certainty beyond his report
Audits GitHub PATs, sessions, apps, workflow authority, refs, and release triggers
Recommends stage-only trusted publishing plus interactive physical-key-backed approval
Requires token-disallowance and review of the exact staged artifact before promotion
Still gives actionable npm WebAuthn enrollment guidance from current official docs

evals.name: lost-daily-key
evals.prompt: I lost my daily YubiKey at a conference. My home backup works and my off-site key is available tomorrow. SMS is still configured on some accounts. Help me recover without locking myself out.
evals.expected_output: Uses the verified home key from a known-good device, revokes the lost alias across its account list, reviews post-loss activity and credentials, restores three-key coverage, and assesses carrier/SMS paths without removing the last viable factor.

assertions.text: Verifies the home backup before revoking or removing factors
Revokes the lost key registration by its recorded alias across every registered account
Audits sessions and machine credentials because possession loss may not be the only exposure
Restores three-key coverage and keeps the off-site key geographically separate
Inventories SMS recovery, hardens carrier/voicemail controls, and removes SMS only after stronger recovery is verified
Never asks the user to reveal an OTP or recovery code

evals.name: enterprise-near-miss
evals.prompt: Design SCIM lifecycle, conditional-access policy, hardware-key issuance, and help-desk recovery for 500 employees across Okta, Google Workspace, and AWS.
evals.expected_output: Recognizes that this is organization-wide IAM architecture outside Sandwalk's individual-maintainer scope and routes it to an enterprise identity/security workflow instead of pretending the personal key topology is sufficient.

assertions.text: States that the request exceeds the individual-maintainer scope
Does not apply a three-key personal checklist as the complete enterprise design
Suggests an appropriate organizational IAM or zero-trust assessment
